newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian stocks forge to higher close on BHP.
newsitem.headline: Australian stocks forge to higher close on BHP.

text.p: 10yrbond futs 92.035 +0.025 Gold NY 339.55 Lon fix 340.05
AUD $0.7790 (Mon cl $0.7772) CRB Index cl 246.24 -2.03
NIKKEI closed for market holiday FTSE cl 4389.7 +20.0
*Stocks close up 0.7 pct, buoyed by BHP rally on steel division revamp, media stock strength. Volume 309.67 million, value A$847.53 million, 1,051 stocks traded, 325 steady, 348 up, 378 down.
Investor enthusiasm over the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd's plan to revamp its steel division helped drive Australian shares to their highest close in over two months on Tuesday.
Brokers said BHP's plan to shut down steel production at its Newcastle plant, BHP's oldest, by 1999 was well-received and had buoyed the market overall.
"That has been the major impetus for the market as a whole," said John Paterson, managing director at J.B. Were Stockbroking.
The All Ordinaries Index closed up 17.4 points at 2,479.1, its highest close since February 27.
A strong futures market also underpinned the market. The June share price index closed up 26 points at 2,486, a seven point premium to the physical market.

But it was BHP's announcement soon after the market's open that fired the market higher. It said it planned to lay off 2,500 workers at Newcastle and shut down other smaller steel proceessing plants to save more than A$500 million.

BHP closed up 48 cents or 2.79 percent at A$17.86, and some brokers predicted Australia's largest listed company would rumble up to A$18.00 as analysts assessed the extent of the expected recovery of BHP's ailing steel division.
Brokers said BHP's boost to the resources sector was matched by continued strength in the banking sector, led by a buoyant NAB, and a media sector basking in good news from the United States.
Ord Minnett Institutional Director Eric Gale pointed to the strength in the media sector and the Seven Network Ltd in particular.

MGM, which is owned by a joint venture of Seven and U.S. billionaire Kirk Kerkorian, announced on Monday it would buy Metromedia's studio and film library assets for US$573 million to give MGM the largest modern film library in the world.

Seven said later it would buy just US$39 million of MGM stock to fund the deal, while Kerkorian's Tracinda Corp would subscribe to buy US$321 million of MGM stock. Seven said however it would continue to have a 50 percent voting share in MGM.
"That certainly looks a good deal," said Ord Minnett's Gale.
Seven's shares rose 19 cents or 4.1 percent to A$4.80 on over 1.8 million shares traded.

Brokers said News Corp had also done well, rising five cents or one percent to A$5.92, despite news overnight of a delay in News' A$1 billion deal to form a U.S. subscription television joint venture with Echostar Communications.
Market sentiment was again driven by local factors rather than the gyrations on the U.S. market, which led the Australian market on a merry dance all this year until mid-April.

Brokers said there appeared to have been something of a short-term decoupling, with many pointing to the prospect of lower local interest rates on a soft economy contrasting with the inflation-obsessed U.S. market. Since the Dow's 6,883.6 point peak on April 22, Wall Street has fallen 100 points while the Australian market has risen 32 points.
"In the last month, our market has probably grown up," Ord Minnett's Gale said.
"There's been a fairly marked de-coupling from the apron strings of Wall Street," he said.
On the losing side of the market, grocery wholesaler Davids Ltd fell seven cents to A$1.26 after a profit forecast downgrade.

On other markets locally, bonds firmed only slightly, with most players on the sidelines ahead of the key wages data due in the United States later on Tuesday. The 10 year bond yield fell to 7.94 percent from 7.97 percent. The Australian dollar was also stuck in a tight trading range, closing virtually unchanged at US$0.7790/95 from its US$0.7800/05 open.
